Moratorium

mor-uh-TOR-ee-um -- five syllables, stress on TOR. · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Moratorium is a temporary halt or suspension of an activity.

After the third accident, the city declared a moratorium on construction permits until new safety codes could be written.

Worked Example

Alarmed by shrinking cod populations, the fishing council orders every boat to stay in harbor for two full seasons while the stocks recover.

That officially declared pause -- fishing halted for a set period, with the expectation that it will resume -- is a moratorium. A moratorium is a deliberate, temporary suspension of an activity, not a permanent end to it.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

suspension: a temporary stop to an activity

freeze: an official halt that locks things in place

postponement: a delay of something to a later time

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

resumption: the act of starting again after a pause

continuation: the act of carrying on without interruption

Where it sits · how sweeping and open-ended the pause is — postponement → moratorium → freeze

postponement vs. moratorium: Postponement is lighter than moratorium -- a postponement pushes one event to a later date, while a moratorium officially halts an entire activity for a period of time.

freeze vs. moratorium: A freeze can bite even harder than a moratorium: a moratorium is a declared pause with the expectation that the activity will resume, while a freeze locks everything in place with no end date in sight.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — mora

Root — mora: delay (Latin mora)

Suffix — -torium

Suffix — -torium: serving to; a thing connected with (Latin -orius/-orium)

Put it together

Put it together: Mora ('delay,' Latin mora) + -torium ('serving to; a thing connected with,' from Latin -orius): Latin moratorius meant 'serving to delay.' A moratorium is literally 'a thing that delays' — an official device for holding an activity in suspension until conditions change.

Use the root in a new word: demur

Use the root in a new word: demur: The treasurer demurred at the sudden expense, putting off her approval until every invoice had been checked.

Root Check

Word Choice

Moratorium takes 'on': a moratorium on testing, a moratorium on new construction, a moratorium on layoffs. It belongs to official, declared pauses by governments, councils, and institutions -- a personal decision to skip dessert for a week is not a moratorium.
